title: The limit of a quotient at infinity

segments.text: Find the limit of two x cubed minus x, divided by x cubed plus four, as x tends to positive infinity. Begin by identifying the form.
Both the numerator and denominator tend to positive infinity. Direct substitution therefore does not determine the result. We need to rewrite the quotient.
The highest power present is x cubed. Divide the entire numerator and denominator by it, including every term, to preserve the value of the quotient.
segments.note: Divide numerator and denominator by x³

segments.text: One over x squared tends to zero, as does four over x cubed. The new denominator tends to one, which is nonzero.
The result is two. We can check it because the degrees are equal and the ratio of the leading coefficients is two divided by one.

courseTitle: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
titleAr: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem
title: Choosing a value that makes a function continuous

segments.text: The function equals x squared minus one divided by x minus one when x differs from one. At one, it has an unknown assigned value a.
For continuity, the value at one must equal the limit. Start by calculating the limit using the expression defined near this point.
Factor the difference of squares. The numerator becomes x minus one times x plus one. Cancel the common factor because x differs from one.
As x approaches one, x plus one tends to two. This is the limit that the function's assigned value must match.
Therefore a must be two. We have filled the gap with the appropriate value. Remember that the limit and the value at the point must agree for continuity.

title: Finding a tangent using both value and slope

segments.text: Let f of x be x cubed minus three x. We want the tangent at the point whose x-coordinate is two.
First find the point's height. Substitute x equal to two to get eight minus six, or two. The point therefore has coordinates two, two.
Now differentiate. The derivative of x cubed is three x squared, and the derivative of minus three x is minus three. This gives the slope function.
At two, the slope is three times four minus three, or nine. Use the tangent formula with the value and slope we have calculated.
segments.note: Use the point and the slope

segments.text: Expand and simplify to get y equal to nine x minus sixteen. Check by substituting x equal to two. We recover two, the point's height.

courseTitle: A complete study of a function
titleAr: A complete study of a function
title: Studying the monotonicity of a cubic function

segments.text: Study where x cubed minus three x increases and decreases. The function is defined on all real numbers, with limits negative and positive infinity at the two ends.
The derivative is three x squared minus three. Factor it as three times x minus one times x plus one.
The derivative vanishes at minus one and one. The product is positive before minus one, negative between them, and positive after one.
The function therefore increases, then decreases, then increases again. Calculate the significant values to obtain two at minus one and minus two at one.
There is a local maximum of two and a local minimum of minus two. The variation table combines these values with the limits so the sketch follows from the calculations.

title: Transforming a sequence into a geometric sequence

segments.text: The initial term u zero is zero, and each new term is half the preceding term plus three. We want a clear method for the formula and the limit.
First look for the number that remains unchanged. Solve ell equal to half ell plus three to obtain six. This is the fixed point.
Set v n equal to u n minus six. Using the recurrence, each new term of v becomes exactly half the preceding term.
The initial value v zero is minus six. Thus v n is minus six times one half to the power n. Add six to return to u.
One half to the power n tends to zero, so u n tends to six. The formula also shows that the sequence is increasing and remains below six.

title: Differentiating an inverse without finding its formula

segments.text: Let f of x be x cubed plus x. We want the derivative of the inverse at two, without finding an explicit formula for that inverse.
The derivative of f is three x squared plus one, which is always positive. Together with continuity and the limits at infinity, this establishes a bijection on the real numbers.
Find the preimage of two. Try one. One cubed plus one equals two, so the inverse evaluated at two is one.
Calculate the derivative at one to obtain four, which is nonzero. We can now apply the inverse derivative formula by taking the reciprocal.
The inverse's derivative at two is one divided by the original derivative at one, or one quarter. Evaluate the original derivative at the preimage, not at the output.

title: Solving a logarithmic equation

segments.text: We want to solve this equation involving two logarithms. First determine the domain, before changing the expression or calculating solutions.
Each logarithm's argument must be positive. Both x minus one and x plus one must be positive, giving x greater than one.
On this domain, combine the logarithms into the logarithm of a product. The product of x minus one and x plus one is a difference of squares.
Because the logarithm is strictly increasing, equal logarithms have equal arguments. Thus x squared minus one equals three, and x squared equals four.
The algebraic equation gives two candidates, two and minus two. We are not finished. Check each candidate against the conditions established at the start.
Minus two is not greater than one, so reject it. Two is admissible, and substitution gives ln one plus ln three. The only solution is two.

title: Solving an equation involving e to the power x

segments.text: This equation contains both e to the power x and e to the power two x. Simplify it by turning it into a quadratic equation in a new variable.
Set t equal to e to the power x. Then t is strictly positive, and e to the power two x is the square of e to the power x.
Now factor the quadratic. Look for two numbers whose sum is three and product is two. They are one and two, giving this factorization.
A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. Thus t equals one or two. Both values are positive and admissible for the substitution.
Return to x. If e to the power x equals one, x is zero. If it equals two, x is ln two.
Substitution in the original equation gives zero for both values. These are the final solutions. The answer must be expressed in x, not left in t.

title: Calculating an integral by parts

segments.text: Calculate the integral from zero to one of x times the exponential. Since the integrand is a product, try integration by parts, one step at a time.
Choose x as the function to differentiate, because its derivative is one. Take an antiderivative of the exponential, which remains the same exponential function.
Apply the formula. Evaluate the product at the limits, then subtract the integral of the exponential. Remember the minus sign, since omitting it changes the answer.
For the first boundary term, substituting x equal to one gives e, and substituting zero gives zero. Their difference is therefore e.
The remaining integral is the exponential from zero to one. Its antiderivative is the exponential, so the upper value minus the lower value gives e minus one.
Finally, subtract e minus one from e, retaining the parentheses. The e terms cancel and one remains. The positive result agrees with the integrand's sign.

title: Solving an equation with an initial condition

segments.text: Solve the equation stating that the function's derivative equals minus twice the function plus six. There is also a condition that its value at zero is one.
Start with the constant solution. A constant has derivative zero, so minus twice this constant plus six must be zero. The constant is three.
The general solution is three plus a constant times e to the power minus two x. Determine this constant using the given initial condition.
Substitute x equal to zero. The exponential becomes one, so three plus the constant equals one. Subtract three from both sides to obtain minus two.
Substitute the constant into the general formula. The solution is three minus twice e to the power minus two x. We still need to check the derivative and the condition.
The derivative is four times the same exponential, which also equals minus twice the function plus six. At zero the value is one, so the solution is correct.

title: Solving a quadratic equation in C

segments.text: Solve z squared minus two z plus five equal to zero. Here the unknown is a complex number. We will work through an organized solution.
First identify the coefficients. The coefficient of the square is one, that of z is minus two, and the constant is five. Now calculate the discriminant.
The discriminant is b squared minus four a c. Here it is four minus twenty, or minus sixteen. Its negative value leads to nonreal complex solutions.
The square root of minus delta is four. The first solution is two plus four i, divided by two. Divide both numerator terms by two.
For the second solution, change the sign of the imaginary part. Two minus four i divided by two gives one minus two i, the conjugate of the first root.
The solutions are conjugates. Check that their sum is two and their product is five, as required by the equation. This verifies the calculation before moving on.

title: A right isosceles triangle using complex coordinates

segments.text: There are three points in the complex plane. A has coordinate one plus i, B has three plus i, and C has one plus three i.
segments.note: Three points in the complex plane

segments.text: To study the triangle from A, calculate the complex coordinate of vector AB. Subtract A's coordinate from B's to obtain two.
Likewise, the complex coordinate of vector AC is C's coordinate minus A's. The real parts cancel and two i remains.
Now divide two i by two. The quotient is i. The denominator is nonzero, so this division is valid.
The number i has argument pi over two and modulus one. The angle between the vectors is therefore a right angle, and their lengths from A are equal.
segments.note: A right angle and equal lengths

segments.text: The triangle ABC is right-angled and isosceles at A. The calculation established both the angle and the lengths, rather than relying on the sketch.
segments.note: A right isosceles triangle at A

title: The distance between a point and a plane

segments.text: Find the distance from M, with coordinates one, one, one, to the plane whose equation is x plus two y plus two z minus six equal to zero.
First read the normal vector from the coefficients of x, y, and z. It is one, two, two. This vector is nonzero.
Its norm is the square root of one squared plus two squared plus two squared. The sum is nine, whose square root is three.
Substitute M's coordinates into the equation. One plus two plus two minus six gives minus one. This is not yet the distance.
Take the absolute value of minus one and divide by the normal vector's norm. One third is the required distance.
The result is positive, which makes sense because M lies outside the plane. The absolute value is essential. Distance cannot be negative, even when substitution gives a negative value.

title: The circle where a sphere and a plane meet

segments.text: A sphere is centred at the origin with radius five. Find its intersection with the plane z equal to three and calculate the radius of the intersection.
The centre projects onto the plane at H, with coordinates zero, zero, three. The distance from the origin to this point is exactly three.
Three is less than five, so the plane cuts the sphere in a circle. This circle's centre is H, rather than the original sphere's centre.
To find the radius, apply Pythagoras' theorem to the right triangle. The circle's squared radius equals five squared minus three squared.
Twenty-five minus nine is sixteen. The radius is positive, so take the positive square root, which is exactly four.
The result is a circle in the plane z equal to three, centred at zero, zero, three, with radius four. We connected the relative position to distance and then to calculation.
segments.note: A circle with centre H and radius 4

title: Choosing a committee of three

segments.text: There are eight people, and we want a committee of three. There is no chair or secretary, so the members have identical roles.
Answer two questions. Order does not matter, and the same person cannot be chosen twice. This is an unordered selection without repetition.
If we temporarily count ordered choices, there are eight possibilities for the first person, seven for the second, and six for the third. Their product is 336.
Each committee has been counted six times because three names have six possible orders. Correct this overcounting by division.
Divide 336 by six to obtain 56 different committees. This agrees with the combination formula.
To choose a formula, always ask about order and repetition. Here the result counts committees. It is neither a probability nor a percentage.

title: Two red balls without replacement

segments.text: A bag contains three red balls and two blue balls, each equally likely to be selected. Draw two successively without returning the first ball to the bag.
We want both the first and second balls to be red. The first-draw probability is three fifths because there are five balls in total.
Now suppose the first ball was red. Two red balls remain, and the total has fallen to four. This information changes the probability on the second draw.
For both events to occur, multiply the first probability by the second conditional probability. We do not multiply three fifths by itself here.
The product is six twentieths. Cancel a factor of two to obtain three tenths, equal to thirty percent of the equally likely cases.
This result depends on sampling without replacement, as the statement specifies. If the ball were replaced, the counts would not fall and the calculation would change.

courseTitle: Random variables and the binomial distribution
titleAr: Random variables and the binomial distribution
title: The probability of two successes in four tosses

segments.text: Toss a fair coin four times independently. X counts heads. We want the probability of obtaining heads exactly twice.
There are four trials, and the success probability in each is one half. Independence and this constant probability allow us to use the binomial distribution.
Choose which two of the four positions will contain successes. The number of choices is four choose two, equal to six.
Each arrangement with two successes and two failures has probability one half squared times one half squared. The product is one sixteenth.
There are six distinct arrangements with the same probability. Multiply six by one sixteenth and simplify to obtain three eighths.
This is the probability of exactly two heads, not at least two. If the wording changes, the events included in the calculation must also change.

title: A Diophantine equation step by step

segments.text: Solve an equation in two unknowns, with the requirement that both solutions be integers. This condition is central to the problem.
The greatest common divisor of eighteen and thirty is six. Since six divides twelve, the equation does have integer solutions.
Divide the entire equation by six to simplify the calculation. We obtain three x plus five y equal to two, without changing the solutions.
Try x equal to minus one and y equal to one. Minus three plus five is two, giving a particular solution from which to build the general family.
Subtract the particular solution and apply Gauss's lemma. We deduce that x plus one is a multiple of five, represented using an integer t.
Substitute x to obtain y equal to one minus three t. The parameter t may be any integer. A final substitution verifies the original equation.

title: Finding the identity and the inverse

segments.text: A new operation on the real numbers adds the two numbers, then subtracts two. To understand it, determine its identity element and its inverses.
The result is a real number for any two real inputs. This simple but necessary check establishes closure of the set.
The identity must leave x unchanged. Write the equation and cancel x on both sides. The identity is two, not zero.
To find the inverse of x, require the result to equal the identity, two. Solving gives four minus x, which is a real number.
Associativity remains to be checked. Evaluate both parenthesizations to obtain the same expression, x plus y plus z minus four, for every three real numbers.
The operation is also commutative, since exchanging x and y changes nothing. Thus we have an abelian group, with every condition checked by calculation.

title: Finding a basis of a vector plane

segments.text: Consider the set of triples whose coordinates sum to zero. We will prove that it is a subspace, then find an explicit basis.
The zero vector belongs to the set. A real linear combination of two solutions still has coordinate sum zero, so closure under linear combinations holds.
segments.equation: 0\in F,\quad u,v\in F\Rightarrow\lambda u+\mu v\in F

segments.text: Choose y and z as free parameters. The equation forces x to equal minus y minus z, giving a parametric representation.
Collect the terms for each parameter separately. Every element becomes s times one vector plus t times another, so these vectors span the space.
To check independence, suppose the combination is the zero vector. The second coordinate forces s to be zero, and the third forces t to be zero as well.
The family is spanning and linearly independent, so it is a basis. It contains two vectors, giving dimension two, even though the elements have three coordinates.

courseTitle: Rolle's theorem, the mean value theorem, and arctangent
titleAr: Rolle's theorem, the mean value theorem, and arctangent
title: Bounding a logarithm with the mean value theorem

segments.text: Bound the natural logarithm of 1.1 without a calculator. Use the logarithm function on the interval from one to 1.1.
The function is continuous on this interval and differentiable inside it because every input is positive. All assumptions of the mean value theorem therefore hold.
On this interval, the derivative lies between ten elevenths and one. The lower bound comes from the largest denominator and the upper bound from the smallest.
The theorem expresses the difference of logarithms as the derivative at an interior point times the interval's width. Here the width is one tenth, which is positive.
Multiply the derivative bounds by one tenth without changing the inequality directions. Then use the fact that ln one equals zero.
We have obtained rigorous bounds from the theorem. We did not need the exact interior point, because the derivative bounds were sufficient to finish.

title: A straightforward proof of adjacency

segments.text: Study two sequences. The first is one minus the reciprocal of n plus one, and the second is one plus that same reciprocal. The initial index is zero.
As the index increases, the denominator grows and the reciprocal decreases. The first sequence subtracts a smaller amount, so it increases at each step.
The second sequence adds a decreasing amount, so it decreases. We now have the required directions, but still need to study the difference.
Subtract the first term from the second. The ones cancel, leaving two divided by n plus one. This quantity tends to zero.
All three conditions hold, so the sequences are adjacent and have a common limit. The number one always remains between the lower and upper bounds.
Find the limit from the formulas or from the sum, which is always two. Its limit is twice the common limit, so the common limit is one.

courseTitle: Integration, integral functions, and Riemann sums
titleAr: Integration, integral functions, and Riemann sums
title: Changing variables and keeping the correct limits

segments.text: Calculate the integral from zero to one of two x divided by one plus x squared. The denominator is positive, so the integral is well defined.
The derivative of the denominator is two x, which appears in the numerator. This suggests choosing the denominator itself as the new variable.
Differentiate the relation to obtain dt equal to two x dx. The numerator together with the differential can therefore be replaced entirely by dt.
Transform the limits as well. When x is zero, t is one, and when x is one, t is two. Do not keep the old limits with the new variable.
The integral becomes one over t, integrated from one to two. Since t is positive on this interval, the antiderivative we need is the logarithm.
Evaluate at the upper limit and subtract the lower-limit value. The logarithm of one is zero, leaving ln two, positive as expected.

title: Solving a quadratic with complex coefficients

segments.text: This quadratic equation has complex coefficients. Begin by calculating delta. There is no need to classify a general complex discriminant as positive or negative.
The leading coefficient is one. To find delta, square two plus i, then subtract four times the constant term, one plus i.
Expand the square using i squared equal to minus one. The imaginary terms cancel on subtraction, leaving delta equal to minus one.
We need a number whose square is delta. The number i works because i squared is minus one. Use i in the formula with both the plus and minus signs.
With the minus sign, the imaginary parts cancel and the result is one. With the plus sign, two plus two i divided by two gives one plus i.
Finally, check the sum and product of the roots. The sum is two plus i, and the product is one plus i, matching the original equation's coefficients.
